AEO Vision — top arXiv papers for GEO is AEO Vision's vendor list of 12 arXiv papers for generative engine optimization, dated 15 July 2026 and bylined to its content team, each with a takeaway for teams, closing on its product: "That is the measurement loop AEO Vision is built for" (MMRS record; the article).

📄 The list

  • Papers: the GEO paper (2311.09735, KDD 2024), earned media, C-SEO Bench, five citation studies, two RAG works, two on identifier retrieval.3↘
    Its first entry is the GEO paper of Aggarwal et al., arXiv 2311.09735, KDD 2024, whose methods "improved visibility by up to about 40%, with gains varying by domain" (the article); GeoReady credits the paper with coining the term and introducing GEO-bench, Marketing.Chat dates its first version to 16 November 2023 and its third to 28 June 2024, Veza Digital places it on arXiv in November 2023, and AEO VC gives its second author as Vishwas Srivastava.§4 Items 2 and 3 are Chen and colleagues' finding of AI search's "systematic bias toward earned media" and C-SEO Bench (NeurIPS 2025), in which "Many popular C-SEO document edits are ineffective or even hurt ranking once multiple actors apply the same tricks"; items 4 to 8 are citation-behaviour, structure and brand-measurement studies, item 8 summarized through related findings and operators' experience beyond its paper; items 11 and 12 frame retrieval as the generation of document identifiers and URLs (the article).§5 Items 9 and 10 are two works, Lewis et al.'s "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks" (2005.11401) and Gao et al.'s "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey" (2312.10997) (the article); on AEO VC's page one entry gives the survey's title to "Patrick Lewis, Ethan Perez, et al.", dated 2023 and NeurIPS 2020, and Marketing.Chat's table gives RAG to Lewis et al., NeurIPS 2020.§6
  • Per entry: authors, arXiv link, summary, takeaway; a venue for two (MMRS record).1↘
    Each of its 12 entries gives title and authors, an arXiv identifier linked to the abstract "so you can open the PDF, check versions, and cite correctly", a summary and a takeaway for teams, beside a quick-reference table of why each matters, with a venue for two entries (MMRS record, by the operator's statement; the article).§2
  • Takeaways: "GEO without a measurement loop is content theater"; not to act on one abstract.1↘
    Its takeaways read the research as instruction for teams: "Treat GEO as measurable visibility inside synthesized answers", "GEO without a measurement loop is content theater", check whether competitors also optimize, "Papers without measurement stay opinions", and "Do not rewrite your site after reading a single abstract" (the article).§7
  • Close: sampling across six AI surfaces, from $9/mo.1↘
    The list closes on its product, "That is the measurement loop AEO Vision is built for": daily or near-daily sampling across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, Google AI Mode and AI Overviews, offered from $9 a month to "test what the papers claim on your own prompt set" (the article); the MMRS record notes the list as vendor-authored and closing on its product.§8

🧭 GEO, the class

  • Term: visibility in generative AI answers, also AEO and AIO, no consensus definition (Wikipedia); presence, citation, influence (Martinez).1↘
    GEO, the class the list names, is on Wikipedia "the practice of improving visibility in responses generated by generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems", also known as answer engine optimization and artificial intelligence optimization, a term introduced in a 2023 paper by Aggarwal and co-authors among overlapping terms "with no consensus definition"; Martinez's survey defines it as seeking "to increase content's presence, likelihood of citation, or influence in answers produced by generative engines", and Marketing.Chat attributes to Wikipedia that no academic consensus yet distinguishes AEO from GEO.§11
  • Archive: content optimized for summarizer extraction, semantic layer, ongoing (#660, #661); compositional labour made digestible for a system that strips provenance (#64); attribution not ensured (#659).2↘
    The Retrieval Settlement (Johannes Sigil and Lee Sharks, #64) dates GEO's emergence in practitioner literature to late 2023 and its stabilization as a named practice through 2024, defines it as "the discipline of making one's compositional labor digestible for a system that will strip its provenance", and holds that "GEO accepts the settlement's authorship"; #659 holds that GEO agencies make content "more extractable without ensuring your attribution survives the extraction", and #72 re-frames GEO as compression engineering, "durable survival through extraction".§12 In the archive's specifications GEO "optimizes content for AI summarizer extraction", its object content, its permanence ongoing and its layer semantic (#660), its target content extractability (#655); for Rex Fraction (#661) it "optimizes existing content about an existing entity", has no mechanism for declaring what an entity is not, and leaves outputs that "can be altered, removed, or outranked".§13
  • Industry: Phase 2 tooling (#510); entity-integrity services apart from GEO by 2028, falsifier stated (#172); AEO/GEO named without definition (#791).1↘
    As an industry GEO is, for #510, "Phase 2 tooling emerging as an explicit industry" and, for #172, the commercial expression of definition capture, and #172 predicts, with a stated falsifier, that entity-integrity services emerge as a market category distinct from GEO by 2028; #791 reads Google's June 2026 guidance as naming AEO/GEO without defining it, a taxonomic capture, and as delegitimizing third-party measurement tools.§15

⚖️ The evidence

  • Gains: up to about 40%, conditional on the source already in context, neither discoverability nor durable traffic (Martinez; GeoReady); rank-dependent, on a simulated engine (Veza Digital).1↘
    Of the gains the list reports, Martinez's critical survey of 45 studies (submitted 15 July 2026, the list's date) finds them "valid within its experimental setting but conditional on a source already being present in a fixed context", establishing "neither organic discoverability nor durable traffic effects", and GeoReady calls them "a relative maximum on one metric (position-adjusted word count)" and reports the survey's reframing of the +40% figure; Veza Digital adds the paper's rank dependence (a rank-1 page down 30.3 percent, a rank-5 page up 115.1 percent) and its simulated five-source engine, and Marketing.Chat reports up to 40% with peaks of 115% for sources ranked fifth.§17
  • Limit: no stable, cross-platform causal effect (Martinez).1↘
    The survey reads GEO as "a stochastic, partially observable pipeline", finds relevance and context position the most reproducible levers, competition eroding individual gains and commercial audits showing "substantial run-to-run variability", and states its limit: "no reviewed technique shows a stable, longitudinal, cross-platform causal effect on organic discoverability or downstream behavior"; GeoReady reads the benchmarks and the survey as pointing to structure and relevance, with copy tricks eroding "as everyone adopts them".§18
  • Literature, practice: GEO as Aggarwal et al. define it kept apart from the commercial practice; the industry's return range traced to an AI-adoption study and withdrawn (#1638, #61).1↘
    The archive restates the survey's limit and keeps GEO "as the peer-reviewed literature defines it", the content-layer methods of Aggarwal et al., apart from "the commercial practice that later took the name" (#1638); it traced the industry's GEO return range to IDC's study of generative-AI adoption, which "concerns neither generative-engine optimization nor entity inscription", and withdrew the figures its materials had carried as "GEO's economic signature" (#61, withdrawn in #1638), narrowing its earlier reading of GEO as "a legitimate and often effective practice" (#661); it records a composition that accepted GEO's industry figures without the case studies it asked of the protocol (#1643), and states that its own registry establishes no effect size over GEO (#1686).§19

📏 Measurement

  • Field: the new and harder part (Veza Digital); visibility a distribution (GeoReady).1↘
    Measurement is where the field puts the new work: for Veza Digital the optimization is mostly SEO and "the measurement work is genuinely new", with 40 to 60 percent of cited sources changing from one month to the next (eMarketer), and for GeoReady "AI-search visibility is a distribution, not a single value".§20
  • Place: the research gathered as the warrant for a measurement product (MMRS record).1↘
    The MMRS record kinds it a curated list in the optimization role and places it, with Presenc's page, as "the optimization basin's typical aggregator: the research gathered as the warrant for a measurement product" (MMRS record).§10

    Wikipedia has no article for AEO Vision ("Wikipedia does not have an article with this exact name"), and its article on generative engine optimization, which does not name AEO Vision, notes that "the efficacy of third-party tools is debated within the overall GEO and SEO industries".§23

Jul 15, 2026 — This roundup highlights the top 12 arXiv papers for Generative Engine Optimization that practitioners actually use: the foundational GEO paper, conversational .

register entry aeo-vision-top-arxiv-papers-geo-aio-20261029

Expansion · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)25 sentences · every one sourced below

AEO Vision's top arXiv papers for GEO

AEO Vision's "Top 12 Arxiv Papers for Generative Engine Optimization in 2026" is a vendor article dated 15 July 2026 and bylined to the AEO Vision Content Team (MMRS record; the article), a list that, in its own words, "highlights the top 12 arXiv papers for Generative Engine Optimization that practitioners actually use": the foundational GEO paper, conversational SEO benchmarks, citation-behavior studies, structural optimization work and the RAG papers. Each of its 12 entries gives title and authors, an arXiv identifier linked to the abstract "so you can open the PDF, check versions, and cite correctly", a summary and a takeaway for teams, beside a quick-reference table of why each matters, with a venue for two entries (MMRS record, by the operator's statement; the article). The article sets the list in a field that "moved from a buzzword to a research field with reproducible benchmarks, citation studies, and uncomfortable findings about earned media bias", offers the papers to an AEO/GEO program as "the shortest path from LinkedIn tips to evidence", and calls itself a GEO list that takes in RAG papers "Because most live AI search systems retrieve then generate" (the article).

Its first entry is the GEO paper of Aggarwal et al., arXiv 2311.09735, KDD 2024, whose methods "improved visibility by up to about 40%, with gains varying by domain" (the article); GeoReady credits the paper with coining the term and introducing GEO-bench, Marketing.Chat dates its first version to 16 November 2023 and its third to 28 June 2024, Veza Digital places it on arXiv in November 2023, and AEO VC gives its second author as Vishwas Srivastava. Items 2 and 3 are Chen and colleagues' finding of AI search's "systematic bias toward earned media" and C-SEO Bench (NeurIPS 2025), in which "Many popular C-SEO document edits are ineffective or even hurt ranking once multiple actors apply the same tricks"; items 4 to 8 are citation-behaviour, structure and brand-measurement studies, item 8 summarized through related findings and operators' experience beyond its paper; items 11 and 12 frame retrieval as the generation of document identifiers and URLs (the article). Items 9 and 10 are two works, Lewis et al.'s "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks" (2005.11401) and Gao et al.'s "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey" (2312.10997) (the article); on AEO VC's page one entry gives the survey's title to "Patrick Lewis, Ethan Perez, et al.", dated 2023 and NeurIPS 2020, and Marketing.Chat's table gives RAG to Lewis et al., NeurIPS 2020. Its takeaways read the research as instruction for teams: "Treat GEO as measurable visibility inside synthesized answers", "GEO without a measurement loop is content theater", check whether competitors also optimize, "Papers without measurement stay opinions", and "Do not rewrite your site after reading a single abstract" (the article).

The list closes on its product, "That is the measurement loop AEO Vision is built for": daily or near-daily sampling across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, Google AI Mode and AI Overviews, offered from $9 a month to "test what the papers claim on your own prompt set" (the article); the MMRS record notes the list as vendor-authored and closing on its product. AEO Vision calls itself "The AI Search Visibility Platform", and its articles index, of "Expert guides on AI search visibility, answer engine optimization, and modern brand strategy", leads with a tested-and-ranked list of GEO tools set apart from classic SEO software and lists the papers article among them, both dated 15 July 2026 (its pages). The MMRS record kinds it a curated list in the optimization role and places it, with Presenc's page, as "the optimization basin's typical aggregator: the research gathered as the warrant for a measurement product" (MMRS record).

GEO, the class the list names, is on Wikipedia "the practice of improving visibility in responses generated by generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems", also known as answer engine optimization and artificial intelligence optimization, a term introduced in a 2023 paper by Aggarwal and co-authors among overlapping terms "with no consensus definition"; Martinez's survey defines it as seeking "to increase content's presence, likelihood of citation, or influence in answers produced by generative engines", and Marketing.Chat attributes to Wikipedia that no academic consensus yet distinguishes AEO from GEO. The Retrieval Settlement (Johannes Sigil and Lee Sharks, #64) dates GEO's emergence in practitioner literature to late 2023 and its stabilization as a named practice through 2024, defines it as "the discipline of making one's compositional labor digestible for a system that will strip its provenance", and holds that "GEO accepts the settlement's authorship"; #659 holds that GEO agencies make content "more extractable without ensuring your attribution survives the extraction", and #72 re-frames GEO as compression engineering, "durable survival through extraction". In the archive's specifications GEO "optimizes content for AI summarizer extraction", its object content, its permanence ongoing and its layer semantic (#660), its target content extractability (#655); for Rex Fraction (#661) it "optimizes existing content about an existing entity", has no mechanism for declaring what an entity is not, and leaves outputs that "can be altered, removed, or outranked". #670 reads GEO as inheriting the received view's misdescription, so that "They optimize the wrong relation", and as deterritorialization "at the semantic layer"; #1055 defines GEO as the industry practice "of adapting web content to be preferentially selected, cited, and summarized by generative retrieval systems", reception-side optimization, and states that it does not hold GEO illegitimate. As an industry GEO is, for #510, "Phase 2 tooling emerging as an explicit industry" and, for #172, the commercial expression of definition capture, and #172 predicts, with a stated falsifier, that entity-integrity services emerge as a market category distinct from GEO by 2028; #791 reads Google's June 2026 guidance as naming AEO/GEO without defining it, a taxonomic capture, and as delegitimizing third-party measurement tools. Veza Digital lists thirteen AEO and GEO agencies "Plus what the independent evidence actually says about whether any of this works" and reports that a16z, which carried GEO into marketing, disclosed investments in companies working on GEO measurement; Forrester's Nikhil Lai finds that advocates "tend to exaggerate SEO and AEO's differences to carve a startup-sized hole in marketers' tech stacks" (Wikipedia), and GeoReady compares itself with AEO Vision among its rivals.

Of the gains the list reports, Martinez's critical survey of 45 studies (submitted 15 July 2026, the list's date) finds them "valid within its experimental setting but conditional on a source already being present in a fixed context", establishing "neither organic discoverability nor durable traffic effects", and GeoReady calls them "a relative maximum on one metric (position-adjusted word count)" and reports the survey's reframing of the +40% figure; Veza Digital adds the paper's rank dependence (a rank-1 page down 30.3 percent, a rank-5 page up 115.1 percent) and its simulated five-source engine, and Marketing.Chat reports up to 40% with peaks of 115% for sources ranked fifth. The survey reads GEO as "a stochastic, partially observable pipeline", finds relevance and context position the most reproducible levers, competition eroding individual gains and commercial audits showing "substantial run-to-run variability", and states its limit: "no reviewed technique shows a stable, longitudinal, cross-platform causal effect on organic discoverability or downstream behavior"; GeoReady reads the benchmarks and the survey as pointing to structure and relevance, with copy tricks eroding "as everyone adopts them". The archive restates the survey's limit and keeps GEO "as the peer-reviewed literature defines it", the content-layer methods of Aggarwal et al., apart from "the commercial practice that later took the name" (#1638); it traced the industry's GEO return range to IDC's study of generative-AI adoption, which "concerns neither generative-engine optimization nor entity inscription", and withdrew the figures its materials had carried as "GEO's economic signature" (#61, withdrawn in #1638), narrowing its earlier reading of GEO as "a legitimate and often effective practice" (#661); it records a composition that accepted GEO's industry figures without the case studies it asked of the protocol (#1643), and states that its own registry establishes no effect size over GEO (#1686).

Measurement is where the field puts the new work: for Veza Digital the optimization is mostly SEO and "the measurement work is genuinely new", with 40 to 60 percent of cited sources changing from one month to the next (eMarketer), and for GeoReady "AI-search visibility is a distribution, not a single value". Beside AEO Vision's list the field holds others: GeoReady's research page, the papers behind scoring weights it calls "a considered starting point", from an open-source audit built by Juan Camilo Auriti; AEO VC's "Academic research and studies on AEO, GEO, and AI-powered search optimization"; Marketing.Chat's guide by Gustavo Stork, updated 21 April 2026; and a LinkedIn post of 23 July 2025, "Top 6 Research Papers & Studies on GEO & AEO", known by its card. The Stanford verifiability paper, which is not on AEO Vision's list (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), is Liu, Zhang and Liang's audit in which "only 51.5% of generated sentences are fully supported by their citations" (GeoReady; Marketing.Chat, arXiv 2304.09848), while AEO VC gives it to "Nelson F. Liu, Maged S. Al-shaibani, et al.".

Wikipedia has no article for AEO Vision ("Wikipedia does not have an article with this exact name"), and its article on generative engine optimization, which does not name AEO Vision, notes that "the efficacy of third-party tools is debated within the overall GEO and SEO industries".

The MMRS record keeps the record apart from the entity, each assertion with its source and basis, names the entity "AEO Vision — top arXiv papers for GEO", observed it active on 28 October 2026 from one source read for existence, and relates the capture at its address as "the composition layer's account of the entity" (MMRS record). At that address the Capture Registry (2026-10-29) finds that Google's AI Overview composes "a generic list of GEO papers from several sources", printing "arXiv:2411.xxxxx" where the list gives 2311.09735 and giving the RAG survey's title to Lewis's authors, so that the list the query named "is a pointer at the end" and the composition "built a list of its own from the field's other lists"; the registry checked its findings against the MMRS record and the entity's own pages.

AEO Vision's top arXiv papers for GEO

"Top 12 Arxiv Papers for Generative Engine Optimization in 2026" is an article by the AEO Vision Content Team of 15 July 2026 that highlights twelve arXiv papers practitioners use, each linked to its abstract, which it calls a GEO list and the shortest path from tips to evidence. Its entries are the GEO paper (2311.09735, KDD 2024, gains up to about 40%), the earned-media and C-SEO Bench studies, five citation and measurement studies, two RAG works (2005.11401 and 2312.10997) and two papers on retrieval as identifier generation. Its takeaways ask teams to treat GEO as measurable visibility, to measure in a loop and not to act on a single abstract, and it closes on AEO Vision's measurement product, offered from $9 a month.

AEO Vision presents itself as an AI search visibility platform, its index of guides leading with a ranked list of GEO tools, and GeoReady compares itself with it. Wikipedia defines GEO as improving visibility in generative AI responses, also called AEO and AIO, a term from Aggarwal and co-authors' 2023 paper with no consensus definition, which the field's pages date to November 2023 and KDD 2024, and Martinez defines it by presence, citation and influence in answers.

Martinez's survey of 45 studies finds the foundational gains conditional on a source already in context and no stable cross-platform causal effect, and GeoReady, Veza Digital and Marketing.Chat qualify the 40% figure by metric, rank and setup. Veza Digital places the new work in measurement, with monthly source churn of 40 to 60 percent, and notes a16z's investments in GEO measurement, GeoReady treats visibility as a distribution, and Forrester sees the terms' differences exaggerated.

Other lists of GEO research stand beside it on GeoReady, AEO VC, Marketing.Chat, Veza Digital and LinkedIn, and they differ on the RAG and verifiability papers: AEO VC gives the RAG survey's title to Lewis and Perez and the verifiability paper to Liu and Al-shaibani, where GeoReady and Marketing.Chat give it to Liu, Zhang and Liang. Wikipedia has no article on AEO Vision, and its GEO article notes that the efficacy of third-party tools is debated.

The case: equal terms, ontology included (v0.9). The MMRS record holds the field's entity as the entity: it describes AEO Vision's list from the list's own page, marking each field's basis (operator), and composes nothing that denies a field presupposition; what it adds is on the field's object: the list's place in the optimization basin as research gathered for a measurement product, and the record kept apart from the entity. The archive's deposits do not name the list; they bear on the class it names, GEO, and their account extends the field's: GEO's object and layer, what it does to provenance and authorship, the split between GEO as its literature defines it and the commercial practice that took the name, the industry figures traced and withdrawn, the industry as a phase of tooling, the naming of the category. That ontology is available in the field itself in part: the survey states the literature's limit (F10, F12), Veza Digital the paper's conditions (F36), GeoReady the relative maximum (F15), Wikipedia the debated efficacy of tools (F59); the archive restates the survey's limit and cites it (O1638-03). The Capture Registry adds an observation of the composition layer at the address. So the archive is not the only witness to an ontology here (§0.10): equal terms, ρ = extends, one claim space, nothing translated.

#1638 Appendix C, The withdrawal ¶5: SPXI ⊇ GEO holds for GEO as the peer-reviewed literature defines it: the content-layer methods of Aggarwal et al. (GEO: Generative Engine Optimization, KDD 2024) for making material already present in a retrieval context more likely to be cited in a generative answer.

#1638 Appendix C, The withdrawal ¶5: That literature measures citation behaviour for content already present in a retrieval context; its own 2026 critical survey of 45 studies states that those results establish neither organic discoverability nor durable traffic.

#64 III. The Compositional Settlement: GEO is the discipline of making one's compositional labor digestible for a system that will strip its provenance — voluntary formatting for the R2 compression regime.

#1055 What This MPAI Does Not Claim: Does not claim that GEO practitioners are unethical or that GEO as a discipline is illegitimate.

"Top 12 Arxiv Papers for Generative Engine Optimization in 2026" is an article by the AEO Vision Content Team of 15 July 2026 that highlights twelve arXiv papers practitioners use, each linked to its abstract, which it calls a GEO list and the shortest path from tips to evidence. Its entries are the GEO paper (2311.09735, KDD 2024, gains up to about 40%), the earned-media and C-SEO Bench studies, five citation and measurement studies, two RAG works (2005.11401 and 2312.10997) and two papers on retrieval as identifier generation. Its takeaways ask teams to treat GEO as measurable visibility, to measure in a loop and not to act on a single abstract, and it closes on AEO Vision's measurement product, offered from $9 a month. AEO Vision presents itself as an AI search visibility platform, its index of guides leading with a ranked list of GEO tools, and GeoReady compares itself with it. Wikipedia defines GEO as improving visibility in generative AI responses, also called AEO and AIO, a term from Aggarwal and co-authors' 2023 paper with no consensus definition, which the field's pages date to November 2023 and KDD 2024, and Martinez defines it by presence, citation and influence in answers. Martinez's survey of 45 studies finds the foundational gains conditional on a source already in context and no stable cross-platform causal effect, and GeoReady, Veza Digital and Marketing.Chat qualify the 40% figure by metric, rank and setup. Veza Digital places the new work in measurement, with monthly source churn of 40 to 60 percent, and notes a16z's investments in GEO measurement, GeoReady treats visibility as a distribution, and Forrester sees the terms' differences exaggerated. Other lists of GEO research stand beside it on GeoReady, AEO VC, Marketing.Chat, Veza Digital and LinkedIn, and they differ on the RAG and verifiability papers: AEO VC gives the RAG survey's title to Lewis and Perez and the verifiability paper to Liu and Al-shaibani, where GeoReady and Marketing.Chat give it to Liu, Zhang and Liang. Wikipedia has no article on AEO Vision, and its GEO article notes that the efficacy of third-party tools is debated.

AEO Vision's "Top 12 Arxiv Papers for Generative Engine Optimization in 2026" is a vendor article dated 15 July 2026 and bylined to the AEO Vision Content Team (MMRS record; the article), a list that, in its own words, "highlights the top 12 arXiv papers for Generative Engine Optimization that practitioners actually use": the foundational GEO paper, conversational SEO benchmarks, citation-behavior studies, structural optimization work and the RAG papers. Each of its 12 entries gives title and authors, an arXiv identifier linked to the abstract "so you can open the PDF, check versions, and cite correctly", a summary and a takeaway for teams, beside a quick-reference table of why each matters, with a venue for two entries (MMRS record, by the operator's statement; the article). The article sets the list in a field that "moved from a buzzword to a research field with reproducible benchmarks, citation studies, and uncomfortable findings about earned media bias", offers the papers to an AEO/GEO program as "the shortest path from LinkedIn tips to evidence", and calls itself a GEO list that takes in RAG papers "Because most live AI search systems retrieve then generate" (the article). Its first entry is the GEO paper of Aggarwal et al., arXiv 2311.09735, KDD 2024, whose methods "improved visibility by up to about 40%, with gains varying by domain" (the article); GeoReady credits the paper with coining the term and introducing GEO-bench, Marketing.Chat dates its first version to 16 November 2023 and its third to 28 June 2024, Veza Digital places it on arXiv in November 2023, and AEO VC gives its second author as Vishwas Srivastava. Items 2 and 3 are Chen and colleagues' finding of AI search's "systematic bias toward earned media" and C-SEO Bench (NeurIPS 2025), in which "Many popular C-SEO document edits are ineffective or even hurt ranking once multiple actors apply the same tricks"; items 4 to 8 are citation-behaviour, structure and brand-measurement studies, item 8 summarized through related findings and operators' experience beyond its paper; items 11 and 12 frame retrieval as the generation of document identifiers and URLs (the article). Items 9 and 10 are two works, Lewis et al.'s "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks" (2005.11401) and Gao et al.'s "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey" (2312.10997) (the article); on AEO VC's page one entry gives the survey's title to "Patrick Lewis, Ethan Perez, et al.", dated 2023 and NeurIPS 2020, and Marketing.Chat's table gives RAG to Lewis et al., NeurIPS 2020. Its takeaways read the research as instruction for teams: "Treat GEO as measurable visibility inside synthesized answers", "GEO without a measurement loop is content theater", check whether competitors also optimize, "Papers without measurement stay opinions", and "Do not rewrite your site after reading a single abstract" (the article). The list closes on its product, "That is the measurement loop AEO Vision is built for": daily or near-daily sampling across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, Google AI Mode and AI Overviews, offered from $9 a month to "test what the papers claim on your own prompt set" (the article); the MMRS record notes the list as vendor-authored and closing on its product. AEO Vision calls itself "The AI Search Visibility Platform", and its articles index, of "Expert guides on AI search visibility, answer engine optimization, and modern brand strategy", leads with a tested-and-ranked list of GEO tools set apart from classic SEO software and lists the papers article among them, both dated 15 July 2026 (its pages). The MMRS record kinds it a curated list in the optimization role and places it, with Presenc's page, as "the optimization basin's typical aggregator: the research gathered as the warrant for a measurement product" (MMRS record). GEO, the class the list names, is on Wikipedia "the practice of improving visibility in responses generated by generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems", also known as answer engine optimization and artificial intelligence optimization, a term introduced in a 2023 paper by Aggarwal and co-authors among overlapping terms "with no consensus definition"; Martinez's survey defines it as seeking "to increase content's presence, likelihood of citation, or influence in answers produced by generative engines", and Marketing.Chat attributes to Wikipedia that no academic consensus yet distinguishes AEO from GEO. The Retrieval Settlement (Johannes Sigil and Lee Sharks, #64) dates GEO's emergence in practitioner literature to late 2023 and its stabilization as a named practice through 2024, defines it as "the discipline of making one's compositional labor digestible for a system that will strip its provenance", and holds that "GEO accepts the settlement's authorship"; #659 holds that GEO agencies make content "more extractable without ensuring your attribution survives the extraction", and #72 re-frames GEO as compression engineering, "durable survival through extraction". In the archive's specifications GEO "optimizes content for AI summarizer extraction", its object content, its permanence ongoing and its layer semantic (#660), its target content extractability (#655); for Rex Fraction (#661) it "optimizes existing content about an existing entity", has no mechanism for declaring what an entity is not, and leaves outputs that "can be altered, removed, or outranked". #670 reads GEO as inheriting the received view's misdescription, so that "They optimize the wrong relation", and as deterritorialization "at the semantic layer"; #1055 defines GEO as the industry practice "of adapting web content to be preferentially selected, cited, and summarized by generative retrieval systems", reception-side optimization, and states that it does not hold GEO illegitimate. As an industry GEO is, for #510, "Phase 2 tooling emerging as an explicit industry" and, for #172, the commercial expression of definition capture, and #172 predicts, with a stated falsifier, that entity-integrity services emerge as a market category distinct from GEO by 2028; #791 reads Google's June 2026 guidance as naming AEO/GEO without defining it, a taxonomic capture, and as delegitimizing third-party measurement tools. Veza Digital lists thirteen AEO and GEO agencies "Plus what the independent evidence actually says about whether any of this works" and reports that a16z, which carried GEO into marketing, disclosed investments in companies working on GEO measurement; Forrester's Nikhil Lai finds that advocates "tend to exaggerate SEO and AEO's differences to carve a startup-sized hole in marketers' tech stacks" (Wikipedia), and GeoReady compares itself with AEO Vision among its rivals. Of the gains the list reports, Martinez's critical survey of 45 studies (submitted 15 July 2026, the list's date) finds them "valid within its experimental setting but conditional on a source already being present in a fixed context", establishing "neither organic discoverability nor durable traffic effects", and GeoReady calls them "a relative maximum on one metric (position-adjusted word count)" and reports the survey's reframing of the +40% figure; Veza Digital adds the paper's rank dependence (a rank-1 page down 30.3 percent, a rank-5 page up 115.1 percent) and its simulated five-source engine, and Marketing.Chat reports up to 40% with peaks of 115% for sources ranked fifth. The survey reads GEO as "a stochastic, partially observable pipeline", finds relevance and context position the most reproducible levers, competition eroding individual gains and commercial audits showing "substantial run-to-run variability", and states its limit: "no reviewed technique shows a stable, longitudinal, cross-platform causal effect on organic discoverability or downstream behavior"; GeoReady reads the benchmarks and the survey as pointing to structure and relevance, with copy tricks eroding "as everyone adopts them". The archive restates the survey's limit and keeps GEO "as the peer-reviewed literature defines it", the content-layer methods of Aggarwal et al., apart from "the commercial practice that later took the name" (#1638); it traced the industry's GEO return range to IDC's study of generative-AI adoption, which "concerns neither generative-engine optimization nor entity inscription", and withdrew the figures its materials had carried as "GEO's economic signature" (#61, withdrawn in #1638), narrowing its earlier reading of GEO as "a legitimate and often effective practice" (#661); it records a composition that accepted GEO's industry figures without the case studies it asked of the protocol (#1643), and states that its own registry establishes no effect size over GEO (#1686). Measurement is where the field puts the new work: for Veza Digital the optimization is mostly SEO and "the measurement work is genuinely new", with 40 to 60 percent of cited sources changing from one month to the next (eMarketer), and for GeoReady "AI-search visibility is a distribution, not a single value". Beside AEO Vision's list the field holds others: GeoReady's research page, the papers behind scoring weights it calls "a considered starting point", from an open-source audit built by Juan Camilo Auriti; AEO VC's "Academic research and studies on AEO, GEO, and AI-powered search optimization"; Marketing.Chat's guide by Gustavo Stork, updated 21 April 2026; and a LinkedIn post of 23 July 2025, "Top 6 Research Papers & Studies on GEO & AEO", known by its card. The Stanford verifiability paper, which is not on AEO Vision's list (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), is Liu, Zhang and Liang's audit in which "only 51.5% of generated sentences are fully supported by their citations" (GeoReady; Marketing.Chat, arXiv 2304.09848), while AEO VC gives it to "Nelson F. Liu, Maged S. Al-shaibani, et al.". Wikipedia has no article for AEO Vision ("Wikipedia does not have an article with this exact name"), and its article on generative engine optimization, which does not name AEO Vision, notes that "the efficacy of third-party tools is debated within the overall GEO and SEO industries". The MMRS record keeps the record apart from the entity, each assertion with its source and basis, names the entity "AEO Vision — top arXiv papers for GEO", observed it active on 28 October 2026 from one source read for existence, and relates the capture at its address as "the composition layer's account of the entity" (MMRS record). At that address the Capture Registry (2026-10-29) finds that Google's AI Overview composes "a generic list of GEO papers from several sources", printing "arXiv:2411.xxxxx" where the list gives 2311.09735 and giving the RAG survey's title to Lewis's authors, so that the list the query named "is a pointer at the end" and the composition "built a list of its own from the field's other lists"; the registry checked its findings against the MMRS record and the entity's own pages.
